In the wild, Vanilla planifolia grows by climbing trees in damp tropical lowland forest, from sea level up to about 600 meters. Puerto Rico: A 1940s variant of the Bourbon method: beans are cleansed with a moist towel, then scalded with three 10-second immersions in an 80°C water bath at 30-second intervals, before being wrapped in a blanket and sweated. Daily two-hour sunnings and nightly sweatings continue for about 7 days until supple, followed by indoor air-drying until the beans shrink to one-third of their weight, then conditioning in tin boxes until they reach one-quarter of their original weight. Because of the higher scalding temperature, Puerto Rican vanilla rarely develops surface frosting. Mexico: Two traditional methods are used - sun-wilting (the older method) and oven-wilting (introduced around 1850) - both still used by specialized curing enterprises; the harvest season runs November to January and curing takes about 5 to 6 months. In sun-wilting, sorted beans are killed by about 5 hours in strong sun on mats or racks, then wrapped in blankets and sweated for 12-24 hours in airtight mahogany boxes; beans that fail to darken are oven-wilted instead. This is followed by daily sunnings (2-3 hours) and overnight sweatings for 5-6 days, then less frequent sunning and sweating for 20-30 days (4-8 total sweatings), then about a month of slow indoor drying, and conditioning (bundling of 50, wax paper, metal boxes) for at least 3 months. 18 Other Methods
Apart from the Bourbon method, the Mexican method is also used extensively in vanilla processing elsewhere in the world. It differs from the Bourbon method in that pods are killed by exposure to strong sunlight rather than hot water: pods are left in the shade for 5-7 days and then spread in strong sunlight for about 5 hours to kill them. All other steps follow the same sequence as the Bourbon method. In South India, pods are killed by boiling, then placed in tied polythene bags on a raised platform in strong sunlight for 3 hours; the next day the bag is untied, water drained, and the process repeated for 3 days, after which the sequence from rapid sun drying onward follows the Bourbon method.
